entry.title: Robotics foundations: transforms, kinematics, control and planning

link.title: Robotics foundations: transforms, kinematics, control and planning

entry.content:
Why this matters

Embodied AI is the part of AI that has to move a body through the physical world. Modern robot learning papers talk about “policies”, “action chunks” and “end-effector deltas”, but underneath every one of them sits a stack of classical robotics: coordinate frames, kinematics, dynamics, low-level controllers and planners. A Vision-Language-Action model that outputs a 7-D end-effector command is useless unless something converts that command into joint torques at 1 kHz without hitting joint limits or itself.

This first post of the Embodied AI track is a compact tour of that stack, written for readers who know deep learning, graphics and world models but have little robotics background. If you have done graphics you already know half of it: a robot arm is a scene graph of rigid transforms, and inverse kinematics is the same problem that animators solve for character rigs.

Prerequisites

  • Linear algebra: matrices, rotations, least squares, the SVD.
  • Calculus: partial derivatives, the chain rule.
  • Python and NumPy.
  • Helpful but optional: homogeneous coordinates from a graphics course.

1. Rigid-body transforms and SE(3)

Rotations: SO(3)

The orientation of a rigid body relative to a reference frame is a rotation matrix $R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times3}$ whose columns are the body’s axes expressed in the reference frame. Rotation matrices form the special orthogonal group

\[SO(3) = \{ R \in \mathbb{R}^{3\times 3} \;:\; R^\top R = I,\; \det R = 1 \}.\]

SO(3) is a 3-dimensional manifold, not a vector space: you cannot add two rotations and get a rotation. Common parameterizations are Euler angles (minimal but singular at “gimbal lock”), unit quaternions (4 numbers, double cover, no singularities, the standard in simulators and game engines), and the axis-angle / exponential coordinates $\omega\theta$ with unit axis $\hat\omega$ and angle $\theta$.

For a vector $\omega = (\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3)$ define the skew-symmetric matrix

\[[\omega] = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\omega_3 & \omega_2 \\ \omega_3 & 0 & -\omega_1 \\ -\omega_2 & \omega_1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\omega]\,v = \omega \times v .\]

The matrix exponential maps axis-angle to a rotation (Rodrigues’ formula):

\[R = e^{[\hat\omega]\theta} = I + \sin\theta\,[\hat\omega] + (1-\cos\theta)\,[\hat\omega]^2 .\]

The set of skew-symmetric matrices is the Lie algebra $\mathfrak{so}(3)$, the tangent space of SO(3) at the identity. Angular velocity lives there: if $R(t)$ is a trajectory, then $\dot R R^\top = [\omega_s]$ gives the angular velocity in the fixed (space) frame and $R^\top \dot R = [\omega_b]$ in the body frame.

Rigid motions: SE(3)

A full pose (position $p$ and orientation $R$) is a homogeneous transform

\[T = \begin{bmatrix} R & p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \in SE(3), \qquad T^{-1} = \begin{bmatrix} R^\top & -R^\top p \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.\]

This is exactly the 4x4 model matrix from graphics. Notation that saves a lot of bugs: write $T_{ab}$ for “the pose of frame $b$ expressed in frame $a$”. Then composition chains like dominoes,

\[T_{ac} = T_{ab}\,T_{bc}, \qquad p_a = T_{ab}\, p_b \;\text{(in homogeneous coordinates)}.\]

The robot’s whole “scene graph” (world, base, links, camera, gripper, object) is a tree of such transforms. Hand-eye calibration, for example, is the problem of estimating the fixed $T_{\text{gripper},\text{camera}}$.

Twists and screws

The velocity of a rigid body is a twist $\mathcal{V} = (\omega, v) \in \mathbb{R}^6$, with $[\mathcal{V}] = \begin{bmatrix}[\omega] & v\0&0\end{bmatrix} \in \mathfrak{se}(3)$. Chasles’ theorem says every rigid motion is a rotation about an axis combined with a translation along it, a screw motion, and the exponential map $T = e^{[\mathcal{S}]\theta}$ turns a unit screw axis $\mathcal{S}$ and a distance $\theta$ into an element of SE(3). This is the foundation of the product-of-exponentials (PoE) formula used throughout Modern Robotics. The dual of a twist is a wrench $\mathcal{F} = (m, f)$ (moment and force); power is $\mathcal{F}^\top\mathcal{V}$.

Why care as a learning person? Because action spaces are poses. Predicting a rotation with a network means choosing a representation: Euler angles have discontinuities, quaternions have the $q \equiv -q$ ambiguity, and Zhou et al. (CVPR 2019) showed that a continuous 6-D representation (two columns of $R$, re-orthonormalized) is easier to regress. Many policies (e.g. Diffusion Policy in post 4) use it.

2. Forward kinematics

A serial manipulator is a chain of links connected by joints, usually revolute (R) or prismatic (P). The configuration is the vector of joint values $q \in \mathbb{R}^n$; the set of all configurations is the configuration space (C-space). Forward kinematics (FK) maps $q$ to the end-effector pose:

\[T_{0n}(q) = T_{01}(q_1)\,T_{12}(q_2)\cdots T_{n-1,n}(q_n).\]

Denavit-Hartenberg parameters

Denavit and Hartenberg (1955) showed that by placing frames cleverly, each link transform needs only four numbers. In the standard DH convention the $z_i$ axis is the axis of joint $i+1$ and

\[T_{i-1,i} = \mathrm{Rot}_z(\theta_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_z(d_i)\,\mathrm{Trans}_x(a_i)\,\mathrm{Rot}_x(\alpha_i) = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_i & -\sin\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & \sin\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\cos\theta_i\\ \sin\theta_i & \cos\theta_i\cos\alpha_i & -\cos\theta_i\sin\alpha_i & a_i\sin\theta_i\\ 0 & \sin\alpha_i & \cos\alpha_i & d_i\\ 0&0&0&1 \end{bmatrix}.\]
Parameter Meaning
$a_i$ link length: distance between $z_{i-1}$ and $z_i$ along $x_i$
$\alpha_i$ link twist: angle from $z_{i-1}$ to $z_i$ about $x_i$
$d_i$ link offset: distance along $z_{i-1}$ (variable for a prismatic joint)
$\theta_i$ joint angle about $z_{i-1}$ (variable for a revolute joint)

Beware: there is also a modified DH convention (Craig), used e.g. in Franka Emika’s documentation, with a different order of the four elementary transforms. Mixing the two is a classic source of bugs. In practice robots are described with URDF or MJCF files (post 3) that store a full transform per joint, and libraries such as Pinocchio, Drake, MuJoCo or PyBullet compute FK for you. DH is still worth knowing because it makes the structure explicit and is how most textbooks and datasheets present kinematics.

A planar 3-link arm in NumPy

For a planar arm, every $\alpha_i = d_i = 0$, so each DH transform is a rotation by $q_i$ followed by a translation $a_i$ along the new $x$ axis. With absolute angles $c_i = q_1 + \dots + q_i$, the end effector is

\[p_x = \sum_i a_i\cos c_i,\qquad p_y = \sum_i a_i \sin c_i,\qquad \phi = c_n .\] 
import numpy as np

def dh(a, alpha, d, theta):
    """Standard DH transform: Rot_z(theta) Trans_z(d) Trans_x(a) Rot_x(alpha)."""
    ct, st, ca, sa = np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta), np.cos(alpha), np.sin(alpha)
    return np.array([[ct, -st * ca,  st * sa, a * ct],
                     [st,  ct * ca, -ct * sa, a * st],
                     [0.0,     sa,       ca,      d],
                     [0.0,    0.0,      0.0,    1.0]])

LINKS = np.array([1.0, 0.8, 0.5])          # link lengths of a planar 3R arm

def fk(q, links=LINKS):
    """Forward kinematics: returns the 4x4 pose of the end effector and all joint positions."""
    T = np.eye(4)
    pts = [T[:3, 3].copy()]
    for a, theta in zip(links, q):
        T = T @ dh(a, 0.0, 0.0, theta)     # planar arm: alpha = d = 0
        pts.append(T[:3, 3].copy())
    return T, np.array(pts)

def task(q):
    """Task-space coordinates x = (px, py, phi) of the end effector."""
    T, _ = fk(q)
    return np.array([T[0, 3], T[1, 3], np.arctan2(T[1, 0], T[0, 0])])

pts gives every joint position, which is all you need to draw the arm with matplotlib.

3. Jacobians and differential kinematics

FK is nonlinear, but its derivative is linear in the joint velocities:

\[\dot x = J(q)\,\dot q, \qquad J(q) = \frac{\partial x}{\partial q} \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times n}.\]

For our planar arm ($m = n = 3$) the columns are easy to derive by differentiating the sums above:

\[J_{1i} = -\sum_{k\ge i} a_k \sin c_k,\qquad J_{2i} = \sum_{k\ge i} a_k\cos c_k, \qquad J_{3i} = 1 .\]

For a general spatial arm, the geometric Jacobian column of a revolute joint $i$ with unit axis $z_{i-1}$ through point $o_{i-1}$ (both in the base frame) is

\[J_i = \begin{bmatrix} z_{i-1}\times(o_n - o_{i-1}) \\ z_{i-1}\end{bmatrix},\]

stacking linear velocity over angular velocity; a prismatic joint contributes $(z_{i-1}, 0)$. (Modern Robotics writes the same thing with space and body Jacobians built from screw axes.)

The Jacobian tells you almost everything about local behaviour:

  • Singularities: where $\operatorname{rank} J < m$ the end effector loses a direction of motion (a fully stretched arm cannot move further outward). Near them, small Cartesian motions require huge joint speeds.
  • Manipulability: Yoshikawa’s measure $w = \sqrt{\det(JJ^\top)}$, the volume of the velocity ellipsoid $\lbrace J\dot q : \lVert\dot q\rVert \le 1 \rbrace$, whose axes come from the SVD of $J$.
  • Statics: by the principle of virtual work, a wrench $\mathcal{F}$ at the end effector requires joint torques $\tau = J^\top(q)\,\mathcal{F}$. This one line is the basis of force and impedance control.
  • Redundancy: if $n > m$ (e.g. a 7-DoF arm for a 6-D pose) there is a null space; joint motions $(I - J^+J)\,z$ move the elbow without moving the hand.

Always test a hand-written Jacobian against finite differences:

def jacobian(q, links=LINKS):
    """Analytic Jacobian d(px, py, phi)/dq of the planar arm."""
    c = np.cumsum(q)                        # absolute link angles
    J = np.zeros((3, len(q)))
    for i in range(len(q)):
        J[0, i] = -np.sum(links[i:] * np.sin(c[i:]))
        J[1, i] = np.sum(links[i:] * np.cos(c[i:]))
        J[2, i] = 1.0
    return J

q = np.array([0.3, -0.5, 0.8])
eps = 1e-6
J_num = np.stack([(task(q + eps * np.eye(3)[i]) - task(q - eps * np.eye(3)[i])) / (2 * eps)
                  for i in range(3)], axis=1)
print("Jacobian error:", np.abs(J_num - jacobian(q)).max())   # ~1e-10

4. Inverse kinematics

Inverse kinematics (IK) asks for $q$ such that \(x(q) = x^{\ast}\). It can have zero, finitely many, or infinitely many solutions.

Analytic IK

For simple or specially designed arms there are closed-form solutions. For a planar 2-link arm reaching $(p_x, p_y)$, the law of cosines gives

\[\cos q_2 = \frac{p_x^2 + p_y^2 - a_1^2 - a_2^2}{2a_1a_2},\qquad q_2 = \pm\arccos(\cdot),\qquad q_1 = \operatorname{atan2}(p_y, p_x) - \operatorname{atan2}(a_2\sin q_2,\; a_1 + a_2\cos q_2),\]

with the $\pm$ selecting “elbow up” or “elbow down”, and no solution when $\lvert\cos q_2\rvert > 1$. Industrial 6-DoF arms with a spherical wrist (last three axes intersecting) decouple into a position problem and an orientation problem (Pieper’s criterion) and have up to 8 analytic solutions. Tools such as IKFast (OpenRAVE) generate these solvers automatically.

Numerical IK: Newton, Jacobian transpose, pseudoinverse

For general arms we iterate. Linearize around the current $q$: \(x^{\ast} - x(q) \approx J\,\Delta q\). Options:

  • Jacobian transpose: $\Delta q = \alpha J^\top e$. Cheap, always a descent direction for $\tfrac12\lVert e\rVert^2$, but slow.
  • Pseudoinverse (Gauss-Newton): $\Delta q = J^+ e$ with $J^+ = J^\top(JJ^\top)^{-1}$ for a wide $J$. Fast near a solution but explodes near singularities because $J^+$ has $1/\sigma_i$ terms.
  • Damped least squares (DLS, Levenberg-Marquardt): minimize $\lVert J\Delta q - e\rVert^2 + \lambda^2\lVert\Delta q\rVert^2$, giving
\[\Delta q = J^\top\left(JJ^\top + \lambda^2 I\right)^{-1} e = \sum_i \frac{\sigma_i}{\sigma_i^2 + \lambda^2}\, v_i u_i^\top e .\]

The SVD form shows why DLS is robust (Nakamura and Hanafusa 1986; Wampler 1986): directions with $\sigma_i \gg \lambda$ behave like the pseudoinverse, while directions with $\sigma_i \to 0$ are damped to zero instead of blowing up. The price is slower convergence and a small bias.

def wrap(a):
    return (a + np.pi) % (2 * np.pi) - np.pi

def ik_dls(x_goal, q0, lam=0.05, iters=200, tol=1e-6):
    """Damped least-squares IK: dq = J^T (J J^T + lam^2 I)^-1 e."""
    q = q0.astype(float).copy()
    for k in range(iters):
        e = x_goal - task(q)
        e[2] = wrap(e[2])                   # angle error must be wrapped
        if np.linalg.norm(e) < tol:
            break
        J = jacobian(q)
        dq = J.T @ np.linalg.solve(J @ J.T + lam**2 * np.eye(3), e)
        q += dq
    return q, k, np.linalg.norm(e)

x_goal = np.array([1.2, 0.9, np.pi / 4])
q_sol, n, err = ik_dls(x_goal, np.zeros(3))
print(np.round(q_sol, 4), n, err)           # converges in ~8 iterations, residual ~1e-7
print(np.round(task(q_sol), 4))             # [1.2, 0.9, 0.7854]

# unreachable target (total reach is 2.3): with lam=0.5 the arm stretches toward it,
# residual 0.7 = the best achievable. With lam=0.05 the iteration oscillates near the singularity.
q_far, n, err = ik_dls(np.array([3.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.1, 0.1, 0.1]), lam=0.5, iters=500)
print(err)                                  # 0.7

Try the last call with lam=0.05: the iterate wanders around with a residual of several units, because the stretched-out arm is singular and lightly-damped steps overshoot. Production IK solvers combine DLS with adaptive damping, step-size limits, joint limits and secondary objectives in the null space; the modern formulation is a small quadratic program (QP) per control tick, e.g. “minimize task error subject to joint position and velocity limits”, solved by libraries such as Pink, mink or Drake.

5. A short look at dynamics

Kinematics ignores forces. The equations of motion of an $n$-joint rigid-body system are

\[M(q)\,\ddot q + C(q,\dot q)\,\dot q + g(q) = \tau + J(q)^\top \mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}},\]

with the symmetric positive-definite mass matrix $M(q)$, Coriolis and centrifugal terms $C\dot q$, gravity $g(q)$, joint torques $\tau$ and external wrenches \(\mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}}\) (e.g. contacts). They come from the Euler-Lagrange equations with Lagrangian $L = \tfrac12 \dot q^\top M(q)\dot q - V(q)$. Two standard problems:

  • Inverse dynamics: given $q, \dot q, \ddot q$, compute $\tau$. The recursive Newton-Euler algorithm (RNEA) does this in $O(n)$.
  • Forward dynamics: given $\tau$, compute $\ddot q = M^{-1}(\tau - C\dot q - g)$. The articulated-body algorithm (ABA) is also $O(n)$ (Featherstone 2008).

Two structural facts make control design possible: $M(q)$ is positive definite, and with a suitable choice of $C$ the matrix $\dot M - 2C$ is skew-symmetric (passivity). Contacts, friction and actuator limits make real dynamics much harder; that is the job of the physics engines in post 3.

6. Control

The controller turns a desired trajectory into torques, typically at 0.5 to 1 kHz on the robot, while a learned policy runs at 5 to 50 Hz on top of it. Knowing which layer your policy commands (joint position targets, joint velocities, end-effector poses, torques) matters a lot for sim-to-real.

PID and PD with gravity compensation

The workhorse is PID on each joint:

\[\tau = K_p\, e + K_i \int_0^t e\, dt' - K_d\,\dot q, \qquad e = q_{\text{ref}} - q .\]

The proportional term acts as a spring, the derivative term as a damper, and the integral term removes steady-state error caused by constant disturbances such as gravity. A better use of a model is PD plus gravity compensation, $\tau = K_p e - K_d\dot q + g(q)$, which for a constant target is globally asymptotically stable (Takegaki and Arimoto 1981). A one-joint pendulum makes the difference visible:

import numpy as np

# 1-DoF pendulum joint: I*qdd + b*qd + m*g*l*sin(q) = tau
I, b, m, g, l = 0.5, 0.1, 1.0, 9.81, 0.5
dt, T = 1e-3, 3.0

def simulate(Kp, Kd, Ki, gravity_comp, q_ref=np.pi / 3):
    q, qd, integ = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0
    for _ in range(int(T / dt)):
        e = q_ref - q
        integ += e * dt
        tau = Kp * e - Kd * qd + Ki * integ
        if gravity_comp:
            tau += m * g * l * np.sin(q)      # feed-forward model term
        qdd = (tau - b * qd - m * g * l * np.sin(q)) / I
        qd += qdd * dt                        # semi-implicit Euler
        q += qd * dt
    return q_ref - q

print("PD only        error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 0, False))   # 0.1861
print("PID            error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 30, False))  # 0.0000
print("PD + gravity   error %.4f rad" % simulate(20, 3, 0, True))    # -0.0001

Plain PD sags by about 0.19 rad because the spring must hold up the weight; the integral term or the gravity model removes the error. Legged-robot RL policies (post 2) almost always output joint position targets to such a PD loop instead of raw torques; the PD gains then become part of the “action space”.

Computed torque and operational-space control

If the model is good, cancel the nonlinear dynamics and impose linear error dynamics (computed torque, or feedback linearization):

\[\tau = M(q)\left(\ddot q_{\text{ref}} + K_d\dot e + K_p e\right) + C\dot q + g .\]

Khatib’s operational-space formulation (1987) does the same in task space. With the task-space inertia $\Lambda(q) = (J M^{-1} J^\top)^{-1}$ the end effector behaves like a body of mass $\Lambda$, and

\[\tau = J^\top\left(\Lambda\,\ddot x_{\text{cmd}} + \mu + p\right) + \left(I - J^\top \bar J^{\top}\right)\tau_0, \qquad \bar J = M^{-1}J^\top\Lambda,\]

where $\mu, p$ are the task-space Coriolis and gravity terms and $\tau_0$ is a secondary objective projected into the dynamically consistent null space (e.g. keep the elbow near a rest pose).

Impedance control

Hogan’s impedance control (1985) does not try to track a position stiffly; it makes the end effector behave like a mass-spring-damper around a target:

\[\Lambda_d\,\ddot{\tilde x} + D_d\,\dot{\tilde x} + K_d\,\tilde x = \mathcal{F}_{\text{ext}},\qquad \tilde x = x - x_d .\]

The simplest implementation ignores the desired inertia and commands $\tau = J^\top\left(K_d (x_d - x) - D_d\,\dot x\right) + g(q)$, using the static relation $\tau = J^\top\mathcal{F}$. Low stiffness gives compliant, safe contact (wiping, insertion, human interaction); high stiffness gives accurate tracking. Many learned manipulation policies output a target pose $x_d$ at 10 to 20 Hz to a Cartesian impedance controller running at 1 kHz; some also predict the stiffness (“variable impedance”).

7. Motion planning

Planning finds a collision-free path in C-space from $q_{\text{start}}$ to $q_{\text{goal}}$. Obstacles in the workspace become complicated “C-obstacles” in joint space, so planners query a collision checker (which runs FK and mesh-mesh tests, the same BVH machinery as in ray tracing) instead of building the free space explicitly.

Graph search: A*

On a discretized C-space (grid or lattice), A* (Hart, Nilsson and Raphael 1968) expands nodes in order of $f(n) = g(n) + h(n)$, cost-so-far plus a heuristic estimate of cost-to-go. If $h$ is admissible (never overestimates) A* returns an optimal path; if it is also consistent (\(h(n) \le c(n,n') + h(n')\)) no node needs to be re-expanded. Dijkstra is A* with $h = 0$. Grids scale exponentially with dimension, so A* is used for mobile robots in 2-D/3-D, footstep planning and discretized lattices, not for 7-DoF arms.

Sampling-based planning: PRM, RRT, RRT*

Sampling-based planners avoid discretization. PRM (Kavraki et al. 1996) samples many collision-free configurations, connects nearby ones and answers queries with graph search. RRT (LaValle 1998) grows a tree from the start: sample $x_{\text{rand}}$, find the nearest tree node, step a fixed distance toward the sample, and add the new node if the edge is collision free. The Voronoi bias of this procedure pulls the tree into unexplored space. RRT is probabilistically complete (it finds a path with probability approaching 1 if one exists) but not optimal. RRT* (Karaman and Frazzoli 2011) adds two steps, choosing the best parent within a shrinking radius $r_n \propto (\log n / n)^{1/d}$ and rewiring neighbours through the new node, which makes it asymptotically optimal.

import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
OBST = [(np.array([0.5, 0.5]), 0.2), (np.array([0.25, 0.8]), 0.12)]   # circles (center, radius)

def free(p):
    return all(np.linalg.norm(p - c) > r for c, r in OBST)

def edge_free(a, b, n=20):
    return all(free(a + t * (b - a)) for t in np.linspace(0, 1, n))

def rrt(start, goal, step=0.05, iters=5000, goal_bias=0.1):
    nodes, parent = [start], [-1]
    for _ in range(iters):
        x_rand = goal if rng.random() < goal_bias else rng.random(2)   # sample in [0,1]^2
        i = int(np.argmin([np.linalg.norm(n - x_rand) for n in nodes]))
        d = x_rand - nodes[i]
        x_new = nodes[i] + d * min(1.0, step / (np.linalg.norm(d) + 1e-12))  # steer
        if not edge_free(nodes[i], x_new):
            continue
        nodes.append(x_new); parent.append(i)
        if np.linalg.norm(x_new - goal) < step and edge_free(x_new, goal):
            nodes.append(goal); parent.append(len(nodes) - 2)
            path, j = [], len(nodes) - 1
            while j != -1:
                path.append(nodes[j]); j = parent[j]
            return np.array(path[::-1]), len(nodes)
    return None, len(nodes)

path, n = rrt(np.array([0.1, 0.1]), np.array([0.9, 0.9]))
print(f"tree size {n}, path waypoints {len(path)}, "
      f"length {np.sum(np.linalg.norm(np.diff(path, axis=0), axis=1)):.3f}")

To plan for the 3-link arm instead of a point, replace the sample space by $[-\pi,\pi]^3$ and free(q) by “FK the links and test each segment against the obstacles”. RRT paths are jagged, so real systems shortcut and smooth them, then time-parameterize them under velocity and acceleration limits (e.g. TOPP-RA). Trajectory optimization methods such as CHOMP (Ratliff et al. 2009) and TrajOpt (Schulman et al. 2013) instead optimize a whole trajectory for smoothness plus collision cost, and GPU-parallel planners like NVIDIA cuRobo bring planning times to milliseconds.

Where learning enters

Classical block Learned replacement or augmentation (later posts)
Hand-designed controller RL policy that outputs PD targets (post 2)
Analytic model Simulator with domain randomization, or a learned world model (posts 3, 5)
Planner + cost function Policy imitating demonstrations, e.g. ACT, Diffusion Policy (post 4)
Task specification in code Language instruction to a VLA model (post 5)

Learning rarely removes the lower layers: an OpenVLA or pi0 policy still sends targets to an IK solver and an impedance or PD controller. Understanding those layers is how you debug a policy that “works in sim but jitters on the robot”.

Try it

The home page Lab has an XPBD cloth demo. Position-based dynamics solves constraints by projecting positions, much like the IK iterations above project an arm onto the “reach the target” constraint; dragging a cloth particle is literally an IK problem for a very redundant chain. A good exercise is to port ik_dls to JavaScript and drag the end effector of a 3-link arm on a canvas.

Representative papers

Paper Venue Year Link Why it matters
Denavit and Hartenberg, A kinematic notation for lower-pair mechanisms based on matrices J. Applied Mechanics 1955 DOI The DH convention
Hart, Nilsson, Raphael, A formal basis for the heuristic determination of minimum cost paths IEEE Trans. SSC 1968 DOI A* search
Hogan, Impedance control: an approach to manipulation, Part I J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Control 1985 DOI Impedance control
Nakamura and Hanafusa, Inverse kinematic solutions with singularity robustness for robot manipulator control J. Dyn. Sys., Meas., Control 1986 - Damped least-squares IK
Khatib, A unified approach for motion and force control of robot manipulators: the operational space formulation IEEE J. Robotics and Automation 1987 DOI Operational-space control
Kavraki et al., Probabilistic roadmaps for path planning in high-dimensional configuration spaces IEEE Trans. Robotics and Automation 1996 DOI PRM
LaValle, Rapidly-exploring random trees: a new tool for path planning Tech. report, Iowa State 1998 - RRT
Karaman and Frazzoli, Sampling-based algorithms for optimal motion planning IJRR 2011 arXiv RRT*, PRM*, asymptotic optimality
Schulman et al., Finding locally optimal, collision-free trajectories with sequential convex optimization RSS 2013 PDF TrajOpt
Zhou et al., On the continuity of rotation representations in neural networks CVPR 2019 arXiv The 6-D rotation representation used by many policies

Learning resources

  • K. Lynch and F. Park, Modern Robotics: Mechanics, Planning, and Control (Cambridge University Press, 2017), free PDF, videos and code on the book page. Chapters 3 to 6 and 8 to 11 cover this post in depth with screw theory.
  • R. Tedrake, Robotic Manipulation and Underactuated Robotics, MIT course notes with runnable Drake notebooks.
  • S. LaValle, Planning Algorithms (Cambridge, 2006), free online.
  • R. Featherstone, Rigid Body Dynamics Algorithms (Springer, 2008), for RNEA/ABA.
  • B. Siciliano, L. Sciavicco, L. Villani, G. Oriolo, Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control (Springer, 2009).
  • Code: Pinocchio (fast rigid-body dynamics), Drake, OMPL (sampling-based planners), Peter Corke’s Robotics Toolbox for Python.

Exercises

  1. Implement the analytic 2-link IK above and check both elbow solutions with fk.
  2. Write the geometric Jacobian for a 3-D arm given by a DH table and verify it with finite differences. Plot the manipulability $\sqrt{\det JJ^\top}$ of the planar arm over its workspace.
  3. Add joint limits to ik_dls by clamping, then by a null-space term that pushes joints to the middle of their range. Compare how often each version reaches random targets.
  4. Extend the pendulum example to a 2-link arm with $M(q)$ and compare PD, PID and computed torque under a 10% error in the link masses.
  5. Turn rrt into RRT* (choose-parent and rewire) and plot path length versus number of samples.

Next: Reinforcement learning for robots, where controllers stop being designed and start being learned.

entry.title: Predict, don’t generate? JEPA, evaluating world models, and open problems

link.title: Predict, don’t generate? JEPA, evaluating world models, and open problems

entry.content:
Why this matters

Posts 3 and 4 were about world models that generate: pixels, tokens or explicit 3D scenes. This last post of the series looks at the strongest counter-position: that an intelligent agent’s world model should predict in an abstract representation space and never reconstruct every pixel. That is the idea behind Yann LeCun’s joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPA). We then ask the question every researcher in this area must answer: how do we know a world model is any good? We finish with open problems and with the bridge to the next series, embodied AI.

Prerequisites

  • Posts 1-4 of this series, in particular the Dreamer vs. MuZero contrast in post 1 (reconstruct vs. predict only what matters).
  • Self-supervised learning basics: Siamese networks, contrastive learning, the representation-collapse problem, exponential-moving-average (EMA) target networks.

1. LeCun’s “A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence”

In June 2022 LeCun circulated a long position paper, “A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence” (version 0.9.2, on OpenReview). It proposes a cognitive architecture made of differentiable modules:

Module Role
Configurator sets up the other modules for the task at hand (executive control)
Perception estimates the current state of the world from sensors
World model predicts future world states, possibly for several imagined action sequences, and fills in missing information
Cost an immutable intrinsic cost (drives such as “pain” or curiosity) plus a trainable critic that predicts future intrinsic cost
Short-term memory stores past and predicted states and their costs
Actor proposes action sequences

The agent can act in two modes. Mode 1 is reactive: perception feeds a policy directly. Mode 2 is deliberate planning: the actor proposes an action sequence, the world model unrolls it, the cost module scores the predicted states, and the actions are optimized by gradient descent or search to minimize total cost, much like model-predictive control. Mode-2 results can be distilled into Mode-1 policies, as Dreamer distills imagination into an actor.

The paper’s central technical claim concerns how the world model should be trained. The world is only partially predictable: the exact position of every leaf on a tree in the wind is not. A generative model that must output pixels has to either model all of that irrelevant randomness or average over it (blur). LeCun argues instead for energy-based models trained to give low energy to compatible pairs $(x, y)$, where $x$ is the observed past and $y$ the future, and for making the prediction in a learned representation space in which unpredictable details can be discarded.

1.1 The JEPA

A joint-embedding predictive architecture encodes both $x$ and $y$, and predicts the embedding of $y$ from that of $x$, optionally with a latent variable $z$ that captures what $x$ cannot determine (or an action $a$):

\[s_x = \mathrm{Enc}_x(x),\qquad s_y = \mathrm{Enc}_y(y),\qquad E(x, y, z) = D\big(s_y,\ \mathrm{Pred}(s_x, z)\big).\]

The danger is representation collapse: if the encoders output a constant, the energy is zero for every pair. Approaches to prevent it fall into two groups:

  • Contrastive methods push up the energy of incompatible pairs (negatives). LeCun argues these scale poorly with the dimension of the representation.
  • Regularized / non-contrastive methods limit the information content of $s_y$ or keep the representation spread out. Examples are VICReg (variance-invariance-covariance regularization), and the asymmetric designs of BYOL, where the target encoder is an EMA copy of the online encoder and receives no gradients.

A hierarchical JEPA (H-JEPA) stacks JEPAs so that higher levels predict further into the future in more abstract representations, which would support hierarchical planning.

The position paper is a research program, not an experiment. The following papers from Meta are its concrete instantiations.

2. I-JEPA: predicting representations of image regions

I-JEPA (Assran et al., “Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture”, CVPR 2023, arXiv:2301.08243) applies the idea to single images, with no hand-crafted data augmentations:

  1. Sample several large target blocks of patches and one large context block (with the target regions removed from it).
  2. A context encoder (ViT) $f_\theta$ processes only the visible context patches.
  3. A target encoder $f_{\bar\theta}$ processes the full image; the target representations are its output tokens at the target positions.
  4. A narrow ViT predictor $g_\phi$ takes the context tokens plus mask tokens with positional embeddings for a target block, and predicts that block’s representations.

The loss is an L2 distance in representation space, averaged over the $M$ target blocks $B_i$:

\[\mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{i=1}^{M} \sum_{j \in B_i} \big\lVert \hat s_{y}(j) - s_{y}(j) \big\rVert_2^2 ,\]

and the target encoder is an EMA of the context encoder, $\bar\theta \leftarrow m\,\bar\theta + (1 - m)\,\theta$, with no gradient flowing into it. The masking strategy turned out to be essential: targets must be large enough to be semantic, and the context must be informative and spatially distributed. Compared with pixel-reconstruction methods such as MAE (He et al., CVPR 2022), I-JEPA learned more semantic off-the-shelf features (better linear probing) with less compute.

3. V-JEPA and V-JEPA 2: from video understanding to planning

3.1 V-JEPA

V-JEPA (Bardes et al., “Revisiting Feature Prediction for Learning Visual Representations from Video”, TMLR 2024, arXiv:2404.08471) extends the recipe to video with spatiotemporal masks (masked regions extend across time, so the model cannot copy from neighboring frames) and an L1 loss in feature space. Trained on about 2 million public videos with no text, negatives, pretrained image encoders or pixel reconstruction, its frozen features were particularly strong on motion-centric tasks such as Something-Something v2, and the paper reports that feature prediction is more label-efficient than pixel prediction.

A follow-up study (Garrido et al., “Intuitive physics understanding emerges from self-supervised pretraining on natural videos”, 2025, arXiv:2502.11831) used the violation-of-expectation paradigm from developmental psychology: show physically possible and impossible versions of the same video and measure the model’s “surprise”, its prediction error in representation space. V-JEPA models were reliably more surprised by impossible events on IntPhys, GRASP and InfLevel, while pixel-generative video models and multimodal LLMs tested in the same study performed close to chance. The authors also note that not every intuitive-physics property is learned well.

3.2 V-JEPA 2 and V-JEPA 2-AC

V-JEPA 2 (Assran et al., “V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning”, 2025, arXiv:2506.09985) scales the approach to over a million hours of internet video plus images and adds the missing ingredient for a world model: actions.

  1. Action-free pre-training of the encoder and predictor on internet video (the V-JEPA objective at scale).
  2. Action-conditioned post-training: the encoder is frozen and a new predictor, V-JEPA 2-AC, is trained on less than 62 hours of unlabeled robot videos (from the DROID dataset) to predict the next frame’s representation from the current representation, the robot’s end-effector state and the action.
  3. Planning: given a goal image, the robot encodes it, and at each step searches (with the cross-entropy method) for an action sequence whose predicted final representation is closest to the goal representation in L1 distance, executes the first action and re-plans (MPC):
\[a^\ast_{1:H} = \arg\min_{a_{1:H}} \Big\lVert \hat s_{H}(s_0, a_{1:H}) - s_{\mathrm{goal}} \Big\rVert_1, \qquad \hat s_{k} = P_\phi(\hat s_{k-1}, a_k).\]

The paper reports zero-shot pick-and-place with Franka arms in two labs that were not in the training data, using only image goals. This is the JEPA program in its most complete form so far: a world model learned mostly from passive video, adapted to control with a small amount of interaction data, and used for planning in latent space.

3.3 Related latent-space planners

  • DINO-WM (Zhou et al., ICML 2025, arXiv:2411.04983) freezes pre-trained DINOv2 patch features and trains only a latent dynamics model on offline trajectories; planning to an image goal with MPC works zero-shot across several manipulation and navigation tasks. It shows that a good frozen visual representation plus a small predictor can be enough, a strong argument for the “predict features, not pixels” view.
  • Navigation World Models (Bar et al., CVPR 2025, arXiv:2412.03572) is the generative counterpoint from the same research circle: a 1B-parameter conditional diffusion Transformer predicts future egocentric frames from past frames and navigation actions, and is used to plan by simulating and ranking candidate trajectories.

4. The predictive-vs-generative debate

Aspect Generative (pixels / tokens) Predictive (JEPA-style latent)
Training signal reconstruct or generate observations match target representations
Unpredictable details must be modeled (diffusion) or averaged (blur) can be dropped by the encoder
Collapse risk none (pixels anchor the representation) real; needs EMA, stop-gradient or variance regularization
Inspectable output yes: you can watch the rollout no: you need probes or a separate decoder
Use as a simulator for humans / data generation natural (Genie, Cosmos) not directly
Compute per prediction high (many denoising steps, many pixels) low (a forward pass in a compact space)
What the representation learns everything needed to render, including texture and lighting what is predictable and shared across views and time
Representative systems Dreamer (with reconstruction), GameNGen, Genie, Sora, NWM MuZero (value-equivalent), TD-MPC2, I-JEPA, V-JEPA 2-AC, DINO-WM

A few observations to keep the debate honest:

  • The lines blur. Latent diffusion models generate in a learned latent space, and their autoencoders already discard imperceptible detail. Dreamer reconstructs pixels but plans in a compact latent. JEPA-style models can be paired with a decoder for visualization.
  • It depends on the use. If the goal is a simulator for humans (games, VR, content creation, synthetic data), pixels are the product. If the goal is control, the evidence from MuZero, TD-MPC2, DINO-WM and V-JEPA 2-AC suggests that reconstruction is unnecessary and possibly harmful.
  • Collapse is the price of not reconstructing. Every non-generative world model needs a mechanism that keeps the representation informative: reward and value prediction (MuZero), EMA targets (I-JEPA), frozen pre-trained encoders (DINO-WM), or explicit variance regularization (VICReg).

4.1 Code: collapse and how EMA targets prevent it

The toy below makes the collapse problem tangible. The “observations” are 1D signals $\sin(\omega u + \varphi)$ with random frequency and phase; the context $x$ is the first half of the signal and the target $y$ is the second half. A JEPA predicts the embedding of $y$ from the embedding of $x$. We compare three variants and report the per-dimension standard deviation of the embeddings across a batch (near zero means collapse) and how well a linear probe on the embedding recovers the hidden frequency $\omega$.

import copy
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

torch.manual_seed(0)
L, D = 32, 16                                   # half-signal length, embedding size

def batch(n):
    omega = torch.rand(n, 1) * 2.5 + 0.5        # hidden factor we hope to recover
    phi = torch.rand(n, 1) * 6.283
    u = torch.arange(2 * L).float()[None]
    s = torch.sin(omega * u * 0.25 + phi) + 0.05 * torch.randn(n, 2 * L)
    return s[:, :L], s[:, L:], omega             # context x, target y, hidden omega

def encoder():
    return nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(L, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, D))

def train(variant, steps=3000):
    enc = encoder()
    pred = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(D, 128), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(128, D))
    target = copy.deepcopy(enc).requires_grad_(False)
    opt = torch.optim.Adam([*enc.parameters(), *pred.parameters()], lr=1e-3)
    for _ in range(steps):
        x, y, _ = batch(256)
        s_x = enc(x)
        if variant == "shared, no stop-grad":
            s_y = enc(y)                          # gradients flow into the target branch
        else:
            with torch.no_grad():
                s_y = target(y)                   # EMA target, stop-gradient
        loss = F.mse_loss(pred(s_x), s_y)
        if variant == "EMA + variance reg.":     # VICReg-style hinge on the per-dim std
            loss = loss + F.relu(1 - s_x.std(0)).mean()
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        with torch.no_grad():                     # EMA update of the target encoder
            for p_t, p in zip(target.parameters(), enc.parameters()):
                p_t.mul_(0.99).add_(0.01 * p)
    return enc

def evaluate(enc):
    with torch.no_grad():
        x, _, omega = batch(4000)
        s = enc(x)
        feats = torch.cat([s, torch.ones(len(s), 1)], 1)
        w = torch.linalg.lstsq(feats[:3000], omega[:3000]).solution
        res = omega[3000:] - feats[3000:] @ w
        r2 = 1 - res.pow(2).mean() / omega[3000:].var()
    return s.std(0).mean().item(), r2.item()

for variant in ["shared, no stop-grad", "EMA target", "EMA + variance reg."]:
    std, r2 = evaluate(train(variant))
    print(f"{variant:>22}: embedding std {std:.4f}, linear-probe R^2 for omega {r2:.2f}")

With a shared encoder and gradients through both branches, the easiest way to drive the loss to zero is to map everything to the same point, and the embedding standard deviation shrinks toward zero. The asymmetric EMA target slows this dynamic down, and the variance term rules collapse out explicitly; compare how much information about $\omega$ each variant keeps. Exact numbers depend on the seed and the number of steps, which is itself a lesson: collapse is a training dynamic, not just a property of the loss.

5. How are world models evaluated?

There is no single accepted benchmark. It helps to separate five questions.

5.1 Does it look right? (perceptual quality)

Frame-level FID, video-level FVD (Fréchet video distance), and suites such as VBench (Huang et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2311.17982), which break video quality into dimensions like subject consistency, motion smoothness and aesthetic quality. These are necessary but weak: a model can score well while violating physics.

5.2 Does it obey physics?

  • Violation of expectation: IntPhys (Riochet et al.), GRASP and InfLevel test whether a model is “surprised” by impossible events (Section 3.1).
  • Physion (Bear et al., NeurIPS 2021 Datasets and Benchmarks, arXiv:2106.08261): predict whether two objects will touch in simulated scenes with collisions, stacking, rolling, draping and more, with human data for comparison.
  • Physics-IQ (Motamed et al., WACV 2026, arXiv:2501.09038): real videos of physical events; the model sees the beginning and must continue it, and its continuation is compared with the real future in where, when and how much motion occurs. Its headline finding is that physical understanding in current video generators is severely limited and not explained by visual realism.
  • Controlled synthetic studies such as Kang et al. (ICML 2025, arXiv:2411.02385) separate in-distribution, combinatorial and out-of-distribution generalization (post 3).

5.3 Does it respond to actions? (controllability)

An interactive world model must make actions matter. Genie measures this with $\Delta_t\mathrm{PSNR}$: the difference between the PSNR of frames generated with the latent actions inferred from the real video and frames generated with randomly sampled actions, both compared with the real frames. If the model ignores actions, the difference is zero. Other common checks: train an inverse dynamics model on real data and test whether it recovers the commanded action from generated frames, or measure the error in the resulting camera or agent pose.

5.4 Is it consistent over time? (memory)

Revisit tests: move away and come back along the same path, and compare the two views of the same place (PSNR/LPIPS, or feature matching). Loop closures and 3D reconstruction from the generated video (run SfM and look at reprojection error) test geometric consistency. Explicit 3D worlds (post 4) pass these by construction for static content.

5.5 Is it useful? (downstream tasks)

Ultimately a world model is a tool, and the best evaluation is what it enables:

  • Planning success: goal-reaching rate when planning with the model (DINO-WM, V-JEPA 2-AC, NWM).
  • Policy learning in imagination: return of an agent trained only inside the model, evaluated in the real environment (Dreamer, DIAMOND, UniSim).
  • Policy evaluation: does the success rate of different policies inside the model rank them the same way as real-world trials? A model that ranks policies correctly can replace expensive robot evaluation even if its videos are imperfect.
  • Data generation: does training on synthetic data from the model improve a downstream perception or driving system (the Cosmos and GAIA-1 use case)?

A minimal sketch of the controllability metric, written so that you can plug in any frame generator:

import torch

def psnr(a, b, max_val=1.0):
    mse = torch.mean((a - b) ** 2, dim=tuple(range(1, a.dim())))
    return 10 * torch.log10(max_val ** 2 / mse.clamp(min=1e-10))

def delta_psnr(model, frames, actions, sample_random_actions, t):
    """Genie-style controllability: PSNR with inferred/true actions minus PSNR with random actions.
    frames: [B, T, C, H, W] real video in [0, 1]; model(context, actions) -> predicted frames [B, t, C, H, W]."""
    ctx = frames[:, :1]
    pred_true = model(ctx, actions[:, :t])
    pred_rand = model(ctx, sample_random_actions(actions[:, :t]))
    target = frames[:, t]
    return (psnr(pred_true[:, -1], target) - psnr(pred_rand[:, -1], target)).mean()

# toy check with a "model" that shifts the first frame by the action (perfectly controllable)
def toy_model(ctx, acts):
    out, f = [], ctx[:, 0]
    for k in range(acts.shape[1]):
        f = torch.stack([torch.roll(fi, shifts=int(a), dims=-1) for fi, a in zip(f, acts[:, k])])
        out.append(f)
    return torch.stack(out, 1)

B, T = 8, 5
acts = torch.randint(-2, 3, (B, T))
first = torch.rand(B, 1, 1, 16, 16)
frames = torch.cat([first, toy_model(first, acts)], 1)             # ground-truth video
rand = lambda a: torch.randint(-2, 3, a.shape)
print("delta PSNR (controllable model):", delta_psnr(toy_model, frames, acts, rand, t=T).item())
print("delta PSNR (model that ignores actions):",
      delta_psnr(lambda c, a: c.repeat(1, a.shape[1], 1, 1, 1), frames, acts, rand, t=T).item())

The controllable toy model gets a large positive $\Delta\mathrm{PSNR}$ (perfect predictions with true actions are clamped by the 1e-10 floor, so the value is large but finite), and the model that ignores actions gets exactly zero.

6. Open problems and research directions

  1. Memory and persistence. How should a world model remember a world it has seen for an hour? Candidates: longer contexts with compression, retrieval by pose, explicit 3D/4D state (post 4), or learned latent maps.
  2. Physical and causal grounding. Video data shows correlations; physics requires interventions. Promising ingredients: interaction data from robots and simulators, physics-based inductive biases (particles, simulators in the loop as in PhysGaussian), and evaluation that tests out-of-distribution laws.
  3. A shared action interface. Keyboard inputs, latent actions, end-effector deltas, language: a world model that transfers across embodiments needs actions that mean the same thing across datasets. Latent action models (post 3) are a start.
  4. Uncertainty. Planning against a confident but wrong model is dangerous (post 1’s model exploitation). Calibrated epistemic uncertainty at scale is largely unsolved for large video models.
  5. Choosing the prediction target. Pixels, latent tokens, self-supervised features, or task quantities? Hybrid objectives (e.g. a JEPA-style latent dynamics model plus a lightweight decoder for inspection) are under-explored.
  6. Evaluation that predicts usefulness. Benchmarks that correlate with downstream planning and policy-evaluation performance, rather than with visual quality.
  7. Efficiency. Real-time, high-resolution, long-horizon generation on a single device; this is also where graphics knowledge (level of detail, caching, foveation, explicit primitives) can contribute.
  8. Multi-agent and social worlds. Most current models simulate one controllable agent; other agents with their own goals are treated as noise.

For a researcher at the intersection of graphics, XR/HCI and embodied AI, items 1, 5 and 7 are particularly natural: explicit representations, perception-aware rendering, and interactive evaluation with humans in the loop.

7. Bridge to embodied AI

World models matter most where actions have consequences in the physical world. The next series on this blog, Embodied AI, starts from robotics basics and simulation, and then returns to the ideas of this series from the robot’s side: world models as simulators for sim-to-real transfer, as policy evaluators, as planners (as in V-JEPA 2-AC and DINO-WM), and as the “imagination” inside vision-language-action models.

Representative papers

Paper Venue Year Link Why it matters
A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence (LeCun) OpenReview (position paper) 2022 OpenReview Modular architecture, energy-based models, JEPA
Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL, Grill et al.) NeurIPS 2020 arXiv:2006.07733 EMA target networks avoid collapse without negatives
VICReg: Variance-Invariance-Covariance Regularization for Self-Supervised Learning (Bardes, Ponce, LeCun) ICLR 2022 arXiv:2105.04906 Explicit anti-collapse regularization
Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners (MAE, He et al.) CVPR 2022 arXiv:2111.06377 The pixel-reconstruction baseline JEPA argues against
Self-Supervised Learning from Images with a Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (I-JEPA, Assran et al.) CVPR 2023 arXiv:2301.08243 Feature prediction for images
Revisiting Feature Prediction for Learning Visual Representations from Video (V-JEPA, Bardes et al.) TMLR 2024 arXiv:2404.08471 Feature prediction for video
Intuitive physics understanding emerges from self-supervised pretraining on natural videos (Garrido et al.) arXiv 2025 arXiv:2502.11831 Violation-of-expectation evaluation of V-JEPA
V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning (Assran et al.) arXiv 2025 arXiv:2506.09985 Action-conditioned latent world model for zero-shot robot planning
DINO-WM: World Models on Pre-trained Visual Features enable Zero-shot Planning (Zhou et al.) ICML 2025 arXiv:2411.04983 Planning on frozen DINOv2 features
Navigation World Models (Bar et al.) CVPR 2025 arXiv:2412.03572 Generative (diffusion) world model for navigation planning
Physion: Evaluating Physical Prediction from Vision in Humans and Machines (Bear et al.) NeurIPS Datasets and Benchmarks 2021 arXiv:2106.08261 Physical prediction benchmark with human data
VBench: Comprehensive Benchmark Suite for Video Generative Models (Huang et al.) CVPR 2024 arXiv:2311.17982 Multi-dimensional video quality evaluation
Do generative video models understand physical principles? (Physics-IQ, Motamed et al.) WACV 2026 arXiv:2501.09038 Visual realism does not imply physical understanding

Learning resources

  • Code: I-JEPA, V-JEPA, V-JEPA 2, intuitive-physics evaluation, DINO-WM, Physics-IQ benchmark.
  • LeCun’s position paper itself is long but readable; sections on the architecture and on energy-based models are the core.
  • For self-supervised learning background: Balestriero et al., “A Cookbook of Self-Supervised Learning” (2023), and the relevant chapters of S. Prince, Understanding Deep Learning (udlbook.github.io/udlbook).
  • Stanford CS236 for the generative side of the debate.

Exercises

  1. In the collapse toy, remove the EMA (copy the online encoder’s weights into the target every step, but keep the stop-gradient). Does it collapse? What does this tell you about the role of the predictor and of the EMA?
  2. Add a decoder that reconstructs $y$ from $\mathrm{Pred}(s_x)$ and train it jointly (a generative auxiliary loss). Compare the linear-probe $R^2$ with and without it. When would you expect reconstruction to help, and when to hurt?
  3. Write the V-JEPA 2-AC planning objective as a CEM loop (sample, roll out the predictor, score by L1 distance to the goal embedding, refit). Reuse the CEM description from post 1.
  4. Design a revisit-consistency metric for a video world model: specify the camera path, the comparison metric and a baseline that would score perfectly by cheating. How do you rule out the cheat?
  5. Pick one open problem from Section 6 and write a half-page research proposal: hypothesis, minimal experiment, and how you would evaluate it.

Next: this is the last post of the World Models series. Continue with the Embodied AI series, or go back to post 1 for the foundations.

entry.title: Explicit worlds: 3D and 4D world generation
entry.content:
Why this matters

The video world simulators of post 3 keep the whole world implicitly inside a network and its context window; that is why they forget what is behind you. The opposite design keeps an explicit 3D (or 4D) representation, such as a mesh, a NeRF or a set of 3D Gaussians, and uses generative models only to create or extend it. Once the world exists in 3D, a classical renderer guarantees multi-view consistency, it can be edited object by object, run in real time on a phone or a VR headset, and handed to a physics engine. For readers coming from the Neural Rendering & 3DGS series, this post is where that series meets world models: the representation is the one you already know, and the new question is how to generate it from text or a single image.

Prerequisites

  • Diffusion models, classifier-free guidance and DDIM (post 2).
  • Radiance fields and 3D Gaussian Splatting (Kerbl et al., SIGGRAPH 2023 / ACM TOG 42(4)): differentiable rendering $x = g(\theta, \text{camera})$.
  • Pinhole camera model: intrinsics $K$, camera-to-world pose $[R \mid t]$, unprojection with depth.

1. The core difficulty: no 3D data at internet scale

There are billions of captioned images and videos but only a few million 3D assets and very few large, high-quality 3D scenes. Every method in this post therefore borrows a 2D prior (an image or video diffusion model) and lifts it to 3D. There are four main strategies:

Strategy Idea Examples Speed
Score distillation optimize a 3D representation so that all its renderings look likely under a 2D diffusion model DreamFusion, Magic3D, ProlificDreamer, DreamGaussian minutes to hours per asset
Multi-view generation + reconstruction generate several consistent views with a 3D-aware diffusion model, then reconstruct Zero-1-to-3, MVDream, CAT3D about a minute
Feed-forward 3D a large network directly outputs a 3D representation from an image LRM and successors seconds
Scene growing (inpaint + depth) render the current scene from a new camera, inpaint the holes with a 2D model, lift with monocular depth, fuse Text2Room, LucidDreamer, WonderJourney, WonderWorld seconds to hours per scene

Objects are mostly handled by the first three; scenes and worlds, which are unbounded and need room-scale layout, mostly by the fourth, or by systems that combine all of them (Marble, Section 6).

2. Score distillation sampling (SDS)

2.1 Derivation

DreamFusion (Poole et al., ICLR 2023, arXiv:2209.14988) optimizes NeRF parameters $\theta$ so that a rendering $x = g(\theta)$ from a random camera looks like a sample from a frozen text-to-image diffusion model $\hat\epsilon_\phi(x_t; y, t)$ with prompt $y$. The natural idea is to minimize the diffusion training loss with respect to the image instead of the network:

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}\Big[w(t)\,\big\lVert \hat\epsilon_\phi(\alpha_t x + \sigma_t \epsilon;\ y, t) - \epsilon \big\rVert^2\Big], \qquad x = g(\theta).\]

Its gradient contains the Jacobian of the U-Net, $\partial \hat\epsilon_\phi / \partial x_t$, which is expensive and, as the paper found, works poorly. Dropping it yields the SDS gradient:

\[\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SDS}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon}\Big[w(t)\,\big(\hat\epsilon_\phi(x_t;\ y, t) - \epsilon\big)\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}\Big].\]

Intuitively: add noise to the rendering, ask the diffusion model which noise it “sees”, and push the rendering in the direction that makes the residual $(\hat\epsilon - \epsilon)$ small. The paper shows this is the gradient of a weighted sum of KL divergences between the noised rendering distribution $q(x_t \mid x = g(\theta))$ and the model’s noisy marginal $p_\phi(x_t \mid y)$. Since $\hat\epsilon_\phi \approx -\sigma_t \nabla \ln p_t$ (post 2, Section 5.3), SDS is gradient ascent on the log-density of the noised rendering, averaged over noise levels: it is mode seeking.

2.2 Practical consequences

  • DreamFusion used a very large classifier-free guidance weight ($w = 100$) to get sharp results. Combined with mode seeking, this causes the typical over-saturated, over-smoothed look of SDS assets and low diversity across seeds.
  • The 2D prior has no notion of 3D identity, so each view tries to look like the “canonical” view of the object; the result can have several faces (the Janus problem). View-dependent prompts (“front view”, “back view”) help; 3D-aware priors (Section 3) fix it more fundamentally.
  • Magic3D (Lin et al., CVPR 2023) speeds this up with a coarse-to-fine schedule (a coarse neural field, then a textured mesh optimized with a latent diffusion prior at high resolution).
  • ProlificDreamer (Wang et al., NeurIPS 2023) proposes variational score distillation (VSD): treat the 3D scene as a random variable and replace the noise $\epsilon$ in the SDS residual by the prediction of a second, LoRA-fine-tuned diffusion model that tracks the distribution of the current renderings:
\[\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{VSD}} = \mathbb{E}_{t,\epsilon,c}\Big[w(t)\,\big(\hat\epsilon_{\phi}(x_t;\ y, t) - \hat\epsilon_{\mathrm{lora}}(x_t;\ y, t, c)\big)\,\frac{\partial x}{\partial \theta}\Big],\]

where $c$ is the camera. This works with normal guidance weights (e.g. 7.5) and gives far more detailed and diverse results.

  • DreamGaussian (Tang et al., ICLR 2024) and GaussianDreamer (Yi et al., CVPR 2024) replace NeRF by 3D Gaussians, which renders much faster and makes densification a natural way to grow geometry; DreamGaussian produces a textured mesh in about two minutes.

2.3 A runnable toy: SDS is mode seeking

The script below trains a small 2D diffusion model on a mixture of 8 Gaussians (exactly as in post 2), then treats 512 free 2D points as the “scene” $\theta$, with the identity as the “renderer” $g$, and optimizes them by SDS. Compare the spread of the optimized points with the spread of real samples.

import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

torch.manual_seed(0)
T = 1000
betas = torch.linspace(1e-4, 0.02, T)
alpha_bar = torch.cumprod(1 - betas, dim=0)
ang = torch.arange(8).float() * (2 * math.pi / 8)
CENTERS = 2.0 * torch.stack([torch.cos(ang), torch.sin(ang)], dim=1)

def sample_data(n):
    return CENTERS[torch.randint(0, 8, (n,))] + 0.1 * torch.randn(n, 2)

def temb(t, dim=32):
    freqs = torch.exp(-math.log(10000.0) * torch.arange(dim // 2) / (dim // 2))
    a = t.float()[:, None] * freqs[None]
    return torch.cat([torch.sin(a), torch.cos(a)], 1)

net = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(34, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.SiLU(),
                    nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.SiLU(), nn.Linear(256, 2))
eps_model = lambda x, t: net(torch.cat([x, temb(t)], 1))

# 1) "pretrain" the 2D prior with the DDPM loss
opt = torch.optim.Adam(net.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
for step in range(4000):
    x0, t = sample_data(512), torch.randint(0, T, (512,))
    eps = torch.randn_like(x0)
    ab = alpha_bar[t][:, None]
    loss = ((eps_model(ab.sqrt() * x0 + (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps, t) - eps) ** 2).mean()
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
net.requires_grad_(False)

# 2) score distillation: theta are free parameters, "rendering" x = g(theta) = theta
theta = (0.5 * torch.randn(512, 2)).requires_grad_(True)
opt = torch.optim.Adam([theta], lr=1e-2)
for step in range(2000):
    t_max = int(980 - 930 * step / 2000)                      # anneal the noise level from high to low
    t = torch.randint(20, t_max, (512,))
    eps = torch.randn_like(theta)
    ab = alpha_bar[t][:, None]
    with torch.no_grad():
        x_t = ab.sqrt() * theta + (1 - ab).sqrt() * eps
        grad = eps_model(x_t, t) - eps                       # w(t) = 1
    opt.zero_grad()
    theta.grad = grad                                         # SDS: skip the network Jacobian
    opt.step()

def spread(x):
    d = torch.cdist(x, CENTERS)
    idx = d.argmin(1)
    return (x - CENTERS[idx]).norm(dim=1).mean().item(), idx.unique().numel()

with torch.no_grad():
    s_real, m_real = spread(sample_data(512))
    s_sds, m_sds = spread(theta)
print(f"real data : mean distance to nearest mode {s_real:.3f}, modes covered {m_real}/8")
print(f"SDS points: mean distance to nearest mode {s_sds:.3f}, modes covered {m_sds}/8")

The SDS points end up much closer to the mode centers than real samples are: each point climbs to a nearby density peak instead of reproducing the spread of the distribution. In 3D this is exactly the over-smoothed, “average-looking” texture of SDS assets. (Which modes are covered depends on the initialization, because each particle simply climbs the nearest hill.) Replacing $\epsilon$ in grad by the prediction of a second model trained on the current particles turns this into a toy VSD. Note also the annealed noise schedule in the loop. If $t$ is drawn uniformly over the whole range at every step, the high-noise terms dominate; the noisy marginal at large $t$ is a single blob around the data mean, so the particles are pulled toward the center of the circle instead of onto the modes (try it). Lowering the maximum timestep during optimization, as ProlificDreamer does with its two-stage time schedule, first settles the coarse layout and then the details.

3. 3D-aware priors: multi-view diffusion and feed-forward models

Instead of fighting the 2D prior’s lack of 3D awareness, one can fine-tune it on 3D data so that it understands cameras:

  • Zero-1-to-3 (Liu et al., ICCV 2023) fine-tunes Stable Diffusion to synthesize a novel view of an object given an input image and a relative camera transform; used as an SDS prior it greatly reduces the Janus problem.
  • MVDream (Shi et al., ICLR 2024) generates several views jointly with cross-view attention, so the views are consistent with each other.
  • CAT3D (Gao et al., NeurIPS 2024) generates many consistent novel views of a scene from one or a few images with a multi-view diffusion model, then reconstructs a NeRF-like representation from them, in about a minute.
  • LRM (Hong et al., ICLR 2024) is a large Transformer that maps a single image to a triplane NeRF in a few seconds, trained on large 3D object datasets; many follow-ups output 3D Gaussians directly.
  • Pose-free reconstruction such as DUSt3R (Wang et al., CVPR 2024) predicts dense 3D point maps from image pairs without known cameras, which makes it easy to lift generated images into a common 3D frame.

The general lesson: generate in 2D where the data is, reconstruct in 3D where consistency is needed. That is also how scene generators work.

4. Scene generation by iterative inpainting and lifting

4.1 The loop

Text2Room (Höllein et al., ICCV 2023, arXiv:2303.11989) was the first to generate a room-scale textured mesh from text alone. The loop, shared by most later scene generators, is:

  1. Render the current scene from a new camera pose. Pixels not covered by existing geometry form a mask $M$.
  2. Inpaint the masked region with a text-conditioned 2D inpainting model (Stable Diffusion inpainting).
  3. Estimate depth for the new image with a monocular depth network.
  4. Align the predicted depth to the depth of the existing geometry on the known pixels (monocular depth is only defined up to scale and shift).
  5. Unproject the new pixels into 3D and fuse them into the scene (a mesh in Text2Room; points or Gaussians in later work).

Text2Room splits this into a generation stage with carefully chosen camera trajectories, which lays out the room, and a completion stage that picks additional viewpoints to fill the remaining holes. Viewpoint selection matters: bad trajectories produce stretched geometry at depth discontinuities.

4.2 The geometry, with code

Depth alignment is a least-squares problem over the known pixels $\mathcal{K}$:

\[(s^\ast, b^\ast) = \arg\min_{s, b} \sum_{p \in \mathcal{K}} \big(s\, \hat d_p + b - d_p\big)^2,\]

after which a pixel $(u, v)$ with aligned depth $d = s^\ast \hat d + b^\ast$ is unprojected to the world as

\[X_{\mathrm{world}} = R\, \big(d\, K^{-1} [u, v, 1]^\top\big) + t .\] 
import numpy as np

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
H, W = 48, 64
K = np.array([[60.0, 0, W / 2], [0, 60.0, H / 2], [0, 0, 1]])

# ground-truth depth of a tilted plane (stands in for the true scene)
v, u = np.mgrid[0:H, 0:W]
d_true = 3.0 + 0.02 * u + 0.01 * v

# monocular depth = unknown affine transform of the truth + noise (relative depth)
d_mono = (d_true - 1.2) / 2.5 + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal((H, W))

# pixels already covered by the existing scene (left half) have known depth
known = u < W // 2
A = np.stack([d_mono[known], np.ones(known.sum())], axis=1)
s, b = np.linalg.lstsq(A, d_true[known], rcond=None)[0]
d_aligned = s * d_mono + b
print(f"scale {s:.3f}, shift {b:.3f}; error on NEW pixels: "
      f"{np.abs(d_aligned - d_true)[~known].mean():.4f} (unaligned {np.abs(d_mono - d_true)[~known].mean():.3f})")

def unproject(depth, K, R=np.eye(3), t=np.zeros(3), mask=None):
    """Lift pixels to world-space points: X = R (d K^-1 [u, v, 1]) + t."""
    vv, uu = np.mgrid[0:depth.shape[0], 0:depth.shape[1]]
    pix = np.stack([uu, vv, np.ones_like(uu)], axis=-1).reshape(-1, 3).astype(float)
    rays = pix @ np.linalg.inv(K).T                 # camera-space rays with z = 1
    pts = rays * depth.reshape(-1, 1)
    pts = pts @ R.T + t
    return pts if mask is None else pts[mask.reshape(-1)]

new_points = unproject(d_aligned, K, mask=~known)   # only the inpainted (new) region
print("new points:", new_points.shape, "z range:", new_points[:, 2].min().round(2), new_points[:, 2].max().round(2))

In a real pipeline the alignment is often done per region or with a depth-completion network conditioned on the known depth, because a single global affine fit cannot repair a wrong depth shape. WonderWorld (below) calls its version guided depth diffusion.

4.3 From meshes to Gaussians, and from rooms to journeys

  • LucidDreamer (Chung et al., arXiv:2311.13384, 2023; later in IEEE TVCG) runs a “dreaming” step (inpaint + depth from a new view) and an “alignment” step that merges the new points into the existing point cloud, then uses the point cloud to initialize 3D Gaussian Splatting and optimizes it on the generated images. Its input can be text, RGB or RGB-D, and the result is a domain-free scene that renders in real time. (Not to be confused with the text-to-3D object method of the same name by Liang et al., CVPR 2024.)
  • WonderJourney (Yu et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2312.03884) generates a journey through a long sequence of diverse but connected 3D scenes, starting from an image or text. A large language model writes the description of the next scene, a visual module builds it as a point cloud with inpainting and depth, and a vision-language model checks each result for artifacts and triggers regeneration.
  • WonderWorld (Yu et al., CVPR 2025, arXiv:2406.09394) makes this interactive: a user moves the camera and types what should appear, and a new connected scene is generated in under 10 seconds on a single A6000 GPU. It uses FLAGS (fast layered Gaussian surfels), a geometry-based initialization that needs only a single view and little optimization, layer-wise generation to handle disocclusions, and guided depth diffusion for consistent depth. The authors note that scenes only have front-facing surfaces, so the viewing range is limited.

This family is the closest explicit analog of the interactive video world models of post 3: it is driven by a camera and text, and it grows the world as you explore, but what it grows is a persistent 3D asset.

5. 4D: adding time

A 4D world is a 3D representation plus dynamics. Two common representations: a dynamic NeRF (a time-conditioned field), and deformable 3D Gaussians, where canonical Gaussians are moved by a deformation field $\Delta\mu, \Delta q, \Delta s = D_\psi(\mu, t)$ (as in 4D Gaussian Splatting, Wu et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2310.08528, which renders dynamic captured scenes in real time).

Generation again borrows priors, now including video diffusion models:

  • MAV3D (Singer et al., ICML 2023, arXiv:2301.11280) was the first text-to-4D method: a dynamic NeRF optimized with SDS from a text-to-video model.
  • 4D-fy (Bahmani et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2311.17984) observes a trade-off: image models give good appearance and 3D structure but no motion, video models give motion but weaker appearance and structure. Hybrid SDS alternates gradients from both kinds of priors (plus a 3D-aware prior).
  • Align Your Gaussians (Ling et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2312.13763) uses dynamic 3D Gaussians with deformation fields and composes text-to-image, text-to-video and multi-view diffusion feedback, with an autoregressive scheme to chain longer sequences.
  • Physics as the dynamics model. Instead of distilling motion from video models, one can simulate it: PhysGaussian (Xie et al., CVPR 2024, arXiv:2311.12198) treats Gaussians as continuum particles and integrates them with the material point method, so that the same primitives are both simulated and rendered. This is the explicit-world answer to “video models do not know physics”.

6. World Labs’ Marble and productized world generators

World Labs released Marble as a limited beta in September 2025 and made it publicly available on November 12, 2025. Marble generates persistent, downloadable 3D worlds from text, images, video or coarse 3D layouts, rather than generating frames on the fly. According to the launch post, Gaussian splats are the highest-fidelity representation of a Marble world, and worlds can also be exported as meshes (low-fidelity collider meshes for physics and high-quality meshes). An experimental editor called Chisel lets users block out structure with simple shapes or imported assets and have the model fill in the appearance. No technical paper describes the model, so how it works internally is not public.

Marble is useful as a reference point because it embodies the explicit route end to end: generation produces an asset (splats + meshes) that is then consumed by ordinary graphics and game tooling. The pixel-space route (Genie 3) instead produces an experience that exists only while the model runs.

7. Trade-offs: pixels vs. explicit 3D/4D

Criterion Pixel-space video world model (post 3) Explicit 3D / 4D world
Multi-view consistency learned, approximate; degrades with time guaranteed by the renderer for static content
Memory / persistence limited by context window the representation is the memory
Dynamics, agents, effects rich, learned from video (water, smoke, characters) hard: need 4D generation or an explicit simulator
Physics implicit, often wrong out of distribution can plug into physics engines (meshes, MPM on Gaussians), but materials must be inferred
Editability via prompts / world events, not precise per-object edits, sculpting, relighting, export to engines
Rendering cost at runtime a large network per frame (GPUs/TPUs) rasterization or splatting, real time on consumer hardware and VR
Generality of content anything seen in video mostly static scenes; unbounded and dynamic content is harder
Interactivity with actions native (action-conditioned) requires a game engine or simulator around the asset

The two routes are converging. Video models are being conditioned on explicit 3D signals (camera trajectories, point clouds, depth) to improve consistency, and explicit pipelines increasingly use video models as their prior (CAT3D-style multi-view generation, 4D-fy). A plausible research direction is a hybrid world model: an explicit, persistent 3D/4D state that is updated by learned dynamics and rendered either by splatting or by a generative “neural renderer” for effects the explicit state cannot represent.

8. Try it: an editable explicit world

The Gaussian World tab of the lab on the home page is a toy illustration of the explicit route. Its world is made of around 200,000 3D Gaussians rendered with the 3DGS pipeline (EWA projection, depth sort, alpha compositing). You can type a prompt or pick a preset, then sculpt the terrain, paint materials, place or erase objects, flood the valley, change the time of day and walk through it in first person.

Two honest caveats. First, the generator is procedural, not learned: a keyword-driven program reads the prompt and builds terrain, lakes, forests and villages; a real system would replace it with a learned model such as the scene generators in Section 4. Second, its dynamics (wind, seasons, relighting) are hand-written shaders, not learned. What the demo does show well is the benefit of the explicit route: every edit is local, persistent and immediately consistent from every viewpoint, and rendering runs in real time in a browser, which is precisely what pixel-space world models struggle with.

Representative papers

Learning resources

  • The threestudio framework implements DreamFusion, Magic3D, ProlificDreamer, Zero-1-to-3 guidance and many other SDS variants in one codebase; it is the fastest way to experiment.
  • Project pages with code: Text2Room, LucidDreamer, WonderJourney, WonderWorld, 4DGaussians.
  • World Labs’ blog posts on Marble describe the product and its export formats.
  • For the 3DGS and camera background, the Neural Rendering series on this blog; for diffusion, post 2 and Lilian Weng’s diffusion post.

Exercises

  1. Derive the SDS gradient by differentiating $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{diff}}$ with the chain rule and identifying the term that is dropped. Under what assumption on the U-Net Jacobian would the dropped term vanish in expectation?
  2. In the SDS toy, add a classifier-free-guidance-like scale by multiplying eps_model(x_t, t) - eps by 5 and 20. How do the spread and mode coverage change? Relate this to the over-saturation of DreamFusion’s assets.
  3. Turn the toy into VSD: train a second small denoiser online on the current particles theta and use its prediction in place of eps. Does the spread approach that of the real data?
  4. In the depth-alignment script, replace the planar scene by one with a step discontinuity and a monocular depth that is a nonlinear function of the truth. Where does the global affine fit fail, and how would a local fit help?
  5. Take one row of the trade-off table in Section 7 and design a hybrid system that gets the best of both columns for that row. What would its training data be?

Next: post 5 steps back from generation: JEPA and the predictive-vs-generative debate, how world models are evaluated, and the open problems that lead into embodied AI.
